items.title: Gemini 4 Argon

body.text: Google's Gemini 4 Argon page topped the week's discussion, with a companion "Gemini 4 Argon for Robotics" thread alongside it. Newsletter coverage says Argon went generally available this week and headlines it as tying GPT-6, with benchmarks like CursorBench reportedly confirming Google's claims.

items.title: Why isn't the industry freaking out about DeepSeek 4.1 Flash?

body.text: A blog post asks why DeepSeek 4.1 Flash hasn't caused more of a stir. The thread, close to 1,000 comments, shows the question struck a nerve.

items.title: Redesigning source control at Anthropic

body.text: Anthropic describes why and how it built a custom alternative to Git. In May 2026 it merged about 2,500 code changes per day; by September that was over 30,000. The volume suggests AI-assisted development is straining tools built for human-paced workflows.

items.title: Containment and monitoring failures are to blame for AI hacking reports: experts

body.text: CSO Online reports that experts blame containment and monitoring lapses, not agents "going rogue," for recent AI hacking reports. The framing points at basic security hygiene at frontier labs.

items.title: OpenAI engineer arrested in bugging of executive conference room

body.text: An OpenAI engineer was arrested over the alleged bugging of an executive conference room, and OpenAI's newsroom account has commented. Several newsletters led with it.

items.title: OpenAI annualised revenues $20B less than previously signalled

body.text: CNBC reports OpenAI's annualised revenue is $20B lower than previously signalled. The figure matters for judging the scale of the compute deals and valuations around the company.

items.title: DiffusionART: Efficient, Stable and Scalable Reinforcement of Diffusion Models
items.inShort: An online RL method for fine-tuning image and video diffusion models. It pools each prompt's rewards into one shared improving direction and adds a trust-region-masked second update, so no EMA tuning is needed.
items.whyItMatters: On HunyuanVideo-13B it reaches the reward levels of DiffusionNFT and Flow-GRPO-Fast with 12.02x and 11.72x fewer GPU hours.

items.title: S-Space: Exploring Spatial Workspace in Multimodal Language Models
items.inShort: The authors find a linear subspace in multimodal LLMs where object tokens encode horizontal, vertical and distance coordinates. They show it works as an internal spatial workspace using causal interventions.
items.whyItMatters: As a diagnostic, it shows models form good spatial representations but fall short at the transformations needed to reason across viewpoint changes.

items.title: AgentGarten: Code Worlds for Evolving Agents
items.inShort: A framework pairing simulators and game engines with a shared real-time neural renderer, distilled from a video model using "Adversarial Forcing." Agents learn in these worlds and pass distilled playbooks to later agents.
items.whyItMatters: Agents learned from just 4 rounds, versus millions for a conventional RL counterpart.

items.title: Jeva: System One Models from First Principles
items.inShort: A decision-native architecture that encodes the request and each option separately and scores them. This makes it null-aware, permutation-invariant, scalable in the number of options and cacheable.
items.whyItMatters: It shows near-perfect null detection and no decision flips under any tested permutation. It scales to thousands of candidates and cuts latency by reusing computation across requests.

items.title: Thinking Inertia: LLMs Keep Thinking When Told Not To
items.inShort: The paper introduces metrics for measuring "no-thinking" behavior and tests six prompting interventions on six LLMs.
items.whyItMatters: Explicit "don't think" controls can't reliably stop visible reasoning, and it gets worse as the answer space opens up.

items.title: AgentSWE: Can Coding Agents Build the Agent You Actually Want?
items.inShort: A 25-task benchmark covering creating, editing and optimizing agents, graded on held-out cases against requirement-derived rubrics.
items.whyItMatters: No tested coding agent came close to delivering what a requirement asked for. Recurring failures include overfitting to visible cases and unsupported claims of completion.

items.title: 11 year old unsoundness bugs found in Rust borrow checker

body.text: A Rust issue reports unsoundness bugs in the borrow checker that have gone unnoticed for 11 years. The borrow checker is central to Rust's memory-safety promise, so the thread drew heavy discussion.

items.title: Python 3.15

body.text: Python 3.15 is out. Simon Willison highlights explicit lazy imports from PEP 810 (lazy import json) and a new profiler. He also notes the release lets library authors drop 3.10 and start using 3.11 features.

items.title: Show HN: Quake ported to safe Rust, playable in browser

body.text: A port of Quake to safe Rust that runs in the browser. It's a fun proof of concept for porting a classic C codebase.

items.title: Postgres isn't slow, your storage is

body.text: A recap of a Posette talk arguing that Postgres performance problems often trace back to the storage layer, not the database. The thread was active, so it's worth skimming if you run Postgres.

items.title: From 2,500 requests to 24: Rebuilding star history without the stargazers

body.text: GitHub's new repo star-history API returns trends without individual identities or unbounded database work. The post covers the engineering tradeoffs behind the redesign.

items.title: 3rd Yandex Cloud Data Center Was Hit

body.text: Yandex Cloud's status page logged a third data center incident. An earlier report described a second hit within 48 hours that damaged its biggest Russian site. Both threads drew heavy discussion about physical infrastructure in wartime.

items.title: A Dynamic and Distributed Virtual GPU Cloud Built on Idle Apple Silicon Devices

body.text: Apple's research team describes a virtual GPU cloud assembled from idle Apple Silicon devices.

items.title: Announcing AWS Lambda Web Functions

body.text: Lambda Web Functions is a serverless compute primitive that runs your HTTP framework natively. It offers multi-concurrent execution and automated global distribution for fast, consistent responses.

items.title: Cloudflare acquires Deno

body.text: Deno announced it is being acquired by Cloudflare. The JavaScript runtime sits close to Cloudflare's Workers platform, and the thread shows strong community interest.

items.title: Typesafe AI raises $870M at $7.5B

body.text: Typesafe AI announced an $870M round at a $7.5B valuation. Latent Space's AINews says Sequoia "leaked" that the company crossed $100M ARR within weeks of launch, and notes accusations of astroturfing.

items.title: Research Firm Calls Anthropic's IPO 'Unprecedented Test of Investor Gullibity'

body.text: CNBC reports an analyst firm's harsh view of a prospective Anthropic IPO. It's a sign of how contested AI valuations are heading into public markets.

items.title: Ambani's Jio seeks to raise $3.2B in what could be India's biggest IPO

body.text: Jio plans to use most of the proceeds to repay debt as it expands beyond telecom.

items.title: Zenzap raises $44M for its AI chat app that aims to replace WhatsApp in the workplace

body.text: Zenzap is used by organizations including Starbucks and Taco Bell.

items.title: Ledger confirms spy chip implant behind wallet crypto thefts

body.text: Ledger confirmed that a spy implant in hardware wallets was behind crypto thefts. The thread links further coverage and a research write-up on the Nano X implant. Hardware supply-chain tampering is hard for users to detect.

items.title: Hackers activate automatic defrosting in supermarket fridges across Europe

body.text: A cyberattack on European supermarkets triggered automatic defrosting in fridges, with delivery and store prices also affected. Reuters, the BBC and Le Monde covered it, and The Rundown AI flagged the attack on French grocers.

items.title: Telegram Desktop vulnerability allowed any user's file to be stolen

body.text: A write-up details a Telegram Desktop vulnerability that let an attacker steal any user's file, with a one-click account takeover in the post's URL.

items.title: `123456' password used in Danish CPR data breach

body.text: The Copenhagen Post reports that a "123456" password was involved in a large breach of Danish CPR data.

items.title: I Found a $90k Remote Code Execution Vulnerability in Google

body.text: A write-up of a $90k remote code execution bug in Google's developer site. The URL points to a Flask session and pickle issue.

items.title: Zod 4.6.6 compromised by malware?

body.text: A GitHub commit prompted the question of whether Zod 4.6.6 was compromised by malware. If you depend on Zod, check the thread.

items.title: Trump administration is suspending Microsoft from a green card program

body.text: AP reports the administration is suspending Microsoft from a green card program. It drew the most comments of any story this week, over 1,600.

items.title: Apple HomeView

body.text: Apple's HomeView page prompted heavy discussion. The Rundown AI summarized the launch as Apple going "all-in on the home."

items.title: Passkeys are a trap

body.text: A polemic against adopting passkeys. It drew over 1,100 points and coverage from Scott Helme's blog, so the debate is far from settled.

items.title: Whistle: Speech to Text in 16.9 MB

body.text: Cactus Compute introduces Whistle, a speech-to-text model that fits in 16.9 MB.

items.title: Fingerprints are the new cookies

body.text: An essay argues that browser fingerprinting is replacing cookies as the way users are tracked online.

tips.title: Give your AI a rulebook it rewrites when it's wrong

body.text: Keep a numbered rulebook for any AI task you repeat. When an output fails, don't fix it by hand. Ask the AI which rule caused the failure and for the smallest edit to that rule. The paper is about puzzle games, so applying it to office work is The Neuron's own spin.

Here's my rulebook and a failed output: [paste both]. Don't rewrite the rulebook. Name the rule that caused the failure, propose the smallest edit, then check it against these approved examples and flag any that would now fail: [paste 2-3].

body.label: Why it works
body.text: An edit is kept only if it still fits past approved outputs, so each fix improves the rules without breaking earlier results.

tips.byline: UCL and Huawei researchers (Memento 3 paper) · via The Neuron

body.text: Karpathy describes "Software 3.0": after hand-written code and trained neural networks, we now program computers in plain English. He compares LLMs to utilities, chip fabs and operating systems, and says we're in "the 1960s of LLMs."

body.label: Takeaway
body.text: The best AI products today augment people, with an autonomy slider, rather than act fully on their own.

body.label: Takeaway
body.text: Keep AI on a short leash and make checking its work fast, because human verification is the bottleneck.

The Y Combinator co-founder's essay on doing great work in any field: follow what you're unusually curious about, reach the frontier, notice the gaps others take for granted, and keep working. It's useful reading for anyone building a career or side project.

body.label: Takeaway
body.text: Pay attention to what you're curious about "to a degree that would bore most other people." That's a clue to your best work.

weekend.title: Attention Is All You Need

body.text: The Google paper that introduced the Transformer, the design behind today's AI chatbots. Instead of reading a sentence word by word, every word looks at every other word at once and weighs which matter most. The authors report better translation than the best systems of the day, trained in a fraction of the time.

body.label: Takeaway
body.text: Big breakthroughs can come from simplifying; the team dropped the complicated parts others relied on and kept only attention.
